The request

Subject: Before we penalize Hub C: I need a latency baseline I can defend
SC
VP of Supply Chain Logistics
To: Lead Operations Analytics Consultant (you)
Reply by Tue, Sep 22 · 11:59 PM ET

Hi Operations Analytics team,

Leadership wants to penalize our regional carrier at Hub C and rewrite our delivery SLAs. Before we do either, I need to trust the order file and know which latency number is fair to put in a contract. Please give me evidence with units and denominators, and tell me plainly what the data can't show.

Specifically, I need answers to 5 questions:

  1. 1. Can we trust the order file?
    Our systems write -1 when age is unknown and 999 when latency is unknown. How many of each are in the 10,000 orders, and which fields can we do arithmetic on? Please don't change or delete any source rows.
    Part A
  2. 2. What does a typical order look like?
    Give me the mean, the median and the spread of valid fulfillment latency, in minutes. If the mean and the median disagree, tell me what that means for a typical customer.
    Part B
  3. 3. Which orders are unusually slow?
    Use a standard rule, not gut feel, to mark the slow tail. How many orders cross the line? Before anyone acts on a flag, I need to know what a flag does and doesn't tell us.
    Part C
  4. 4. Is Hub C really different?
    Compare Hub A, Hub B and Hub C using the same rules: order counts, medians and spread. Make sure the hub counts add up to the total.
    Part D
  5. 5. Should we penalize Hub C, and what should the SLA say?
    Tell me whether the mean, the median or the 95th percentile should anchor the SLA, and whether the records support a penalty. Tell me what is still uncertain and what evidence we should collect next. Don't claim a hub caused delays from summaries alone.
    Take-home

Please send me:

  • your completed workbook, and
  • a one-page memo that answers the penalty and SLA questions first, cites every number with its unit (minutes or records) and denominator, and discloses any AI use.

The order extract and the workbook are attached. Thanks. The carrier review depends on this.

Best,
VP of Supply Chain Logistics
Metro E-Commerce Logistics

Windows

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part A · answers email question 1

Part A · Can we trust the order file?

⏱ 6 min
From slide 26 → work this card → Back to slide 27 · bring: Number of sentinel rows identified and confirmed scale of OrderTier.

What the session covered · Section 1 Data Quality, Provenance, and Measurement Scales

Before you average anything, check two things: what each column measures, and which stored values are not measurements at all.

  • Measurement scales: Stevens' four scales decide which arithmetic is allowed. Nominal: count and mode. Ordinal: rank and median. Interval: mean and difference. Ratio: mean and ratio.
  • Digits are not always numbers: an order ID or a code stored as digits can still be a label. How a value is stored does not decide its scale; what it means does.
  • Grain: know what one row represents before you count. In Orders, one row is one recorded order.
  • Sentinel codes: placeholders such as −1 -1 for age and 999 999 for latency mean missing. Count them and exclude them inside formulas. Never delete or overwrite them in the source.
  • Valid denominator: nvalid=N−documented exclusions n_{\text{valid}} = N - \text{documented exclusions} . Every later statistic divides by this number, not by all rows.

Why missingness matters: missing values are MCAR (completely at random), MAR (related to other recorded fields) or MNAR (related to the missing value itself). Dropping rows is only safe when the gaps are close to random, so note where the sentinel rows sit before you exclude them.

Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • #NAME? or #REF! error. The data table must be named Orders with the headers Age_Years and Latency_Minutes. Don't rename the table or its columns.
  • B7 or B8 shows 0. Check the column: -1 lives in Age_Years and 999 lives in Latency_Minutes. Type the criterion as a plain number, e.g. COUNTIF(Orders[Age_Years],-1).
  • Tempted to delete the sentinel rows. Don't. Data must keep all 10,000 rows. The later formulas skip the codes for you with <>999.
Why keep the sentinel rows instead of deleting them? (optional)

Deleting rows destroys the audit trail. Your VP, or a grader, must be able to see the codes and check your rule. Excluding them inside each formula keeps the source intact and makes the rule visible. It also lets you ask why they are missing: if the missing values cluster in one hub or one kind of order, the gaps are not random.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part B · answers email question 2

Part B · What does a typical order look like?

⏱ 7 min
From slide 45 → work this card → Back to slide 46 · bring: Calculated sample median and IQR for fulfillment duration.

What the session covered · Section 2 Describing Distributions: Center, Spread, and Shape

Center and spread answer two different questions: where does a typical order sit, and how much do orders vary around it?

  • Mean: the balance point, xˉ=1n∑xi \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i . Every value pulls on it, so a few very long deliveries move it.
  • Median: the middle ranked value x~ \tilde{x} . Half the orders are faster and half are slower. Its 50% breakdown point means extreme values barely move it.
  • Sample standard deviation: the typical distance from the mean, s=∑(xi−xˉ)2/(n−1) s = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 / (n-1)} . Squaring the distances makes it sensitive to the tail.
  • Interquartile range: the width of the middle half, IQR=Q3−Q1 \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 . Like the median, it resists extreme values.
  • Shape: skewness tells you which side has the longer tail. Comparing the mean with the median is a quick first check. The 68-95-99.7 rule assumes a symmetric, normal shape, so don't apply it to skewed latency.

Stuck? Three quick fixes

The mean adds up every value, so a few very long deliveries pull it up. The median depends only on which order sits in the middle, so it stays put. To watch this happen, try Topic 2 (Resistance) in the optional practice. It adds the 999 codes back in, in the tool of your choice.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part C · answers email question 3

Part C · Which orders are unusually slow?

⏱ 6 min
From slide 67 → work this card → Back to slide 68 · bring: Computed upper fence value and count of flagged delay incidents.

What the session covered · Section 3 Visual Evidence, Honest Displays, and Decluttering

A boxplot draws the middle half of the data as a box and marks unusual values with Tukey fences. Honest charts let the reader see the real shape.

  • Tukey fences: Lower=Q1−1.5 IQR \text{Lower} = Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} and Upper=Q3+1.5 IQR \text{Upper} = Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR} . Values beyond a fence are flagged.
  • Built from resistant pieces: the fences use quartiles, so the extreme values they flag can't drag the fences outward the way they would drag a mean-plus-SD rule.
  • Honest histograms: minutes are continuous, so the bars should touch with no gaps. Bar charts of amounts should start their value axis at zero.
  • Declutter: remove non-data ink (3D effects, heavy gridlines, rainbow colors) and use one highlight color for the point that matters. Data-ink ratio=data ink/total ink \text{Data-ink ratio} = \text{data ink} / \text{total ink} .

Stuck? Three quick fixes
  • #REF! in B7 or B8. Both fences read the IQR from 'IN-CLASS_Lab Part B'!B10. Finish Part B first and don't rename that sheet.
  • B9 looks too high. The 999 codes may be counted as slow orders. Keep all three COUNTIFS criteria: "<>"&999, "<>" and ">"&B7.
  • B10 and B11 are equal. Is that wrong? No. LARGE(...,2) returns the second value in sorted order, and two orders can share the same latency.
Why 1.5 times the IQR? (optional)

Tukey picked 1.5 as a practical rule of thumb. For normal data, the fences sit about 2.7 standard deviations from the mean, so fewer than 1% of values are flagged. Skewed data such as latency flag many more values on the long side. Try other multipliers in Topic 3 (fence sensitivity) in the optional practice.

sheet IN-CLASS_Lab Part D · answers email question 4

Part D · Is Hub C really different?

⏱ 7 min
From slide 86 → work this card → Back to slide 90 · bring: Completed hub counts, medians and IQRs, with count reconciliation.

What the session covered · Section 4 Grouped Summaries, Comparative Distributions, and Lab Practice

To compare groups fairly, keep the data stacked (one row per order, one column for the group) and apply the same rules to every group.

  • Stacked layout: Orders has one row per order, with Hub in one column and Latency_Minutes in another. That is what lets one formula, one PivotTable or one SPSS BY Hub summarize every hub.
  • Audit standard: report each group's sample size, center and spread together, all from the same valid-latency filter and the same quartile rule.
  • Reconcile the counts: the hub counts must add up: nA+nB+nC=nall n_A + n_B + n_C = n_{\text{all}} . If they don't, a filter differs somewhere.
  • Pooled, not averaged: the all-hubs median and IQR come from all valid orders pooled together, not from averaging the three hub values.
  • Causal boundary: a group summary describes the group, not each order in it (the ecological fallacy). A difference between hubs is a description, not proof that a hub caused it.

Take-home · Should we penalize Hub C, and what should the SLA say?

⏱ 60 min
At home → work this card → Submit

What the session covered · Section 4 Grouped Summaries, Comparative Distributions, and Lab Practice

The take-home reuses Parts A to D to answer the VP's two decisions. Each statistic answers a different SLA question:

  • Median: the typical order. It resists the tail.
  • Mean: the average minutes per order. Every minute counts, including the tail, so it can sit well above what a typical customer sees.
  • 95th percentile: the upper-tail threshold: 95% of valid orders are at or below P95 P_{95} . PERCENTILE.EXC(v,0.95) uses the same p (n+1) p\,(n+1) rule as QUARTILE.EXC.
  • Share above a threshold: a proportion of Hub C's own valid orders, so the denominator is nC n_C (B9), not the all-hubs count.
  • Causal boundary: route mix, package mix or geography could also produce a hub difference. Name the evidence that would test a cause.

There are no dropdowns here. Write the evidence defense and the recommendation in your own words, with a unit and a denominator for every number.

Topic 1 · Reproduce the in-class parts Reproduce

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts A, B, C, D

No new formulas. Reopen your finished workbook and work through the sheets IN-CLASS_Lab Part A to IN-CLASS_Lab Part D. Step 1. Read column C next to each answer cell. It should say Result matches. Step 2. Scroll to the Check your work box under each table. Every line should read "✓ Checked". Step 3. If a cell says Check the result, click it and read the formula bar. Most slips are a missing <>999 filter or QUARTILE.INC in place of QUARTILE.EXC. Step 4. On Part D, confirm that B7 + B8 + B9 equals B10, the 9,958 valid orders.

SPSS Parts A, B, C, D

No new syntax. Open LAB01_SPSS.sps, run H0, then run H1 to H4 one block at a time and compare each output with your workbook. H1: the -1 row for Age_Years and the 999 row for Latency_Minutes should each show 42 records (Part A B7:B8). H2: valid N, mean, median and SD match Part B B7:B9. Take Q3 minus Q1 from the HAVERAGE Percentiles table for B10. H3: Q3 + 1.5 times the IQR from that table gives the 49.0-minute fence in Part C B7. Read the boxplot for shape only, since its hinges can differ slightly. H4: each hub's valid N, median, Q1 and Q3 match Part D rows 7 to 9. Stop at H4; H5 belongs to the take-home.

Python Parts A, B, C, D

Counts the sentinel codes, then rebuilds every Part B, C and D value from the valid orders. Your printed numbers should match the workbook checks exactly, for example 9,958 valid orders, a 22.0-minute median, a 49.0-minute upper fence and 829 flagged records. method="weibull" is numpy's name for the QUARTILE.EXC rule. Runs in Colab or any Python with pandas and numpy.

# LAB01 Parts A-D in Python (optional, not graded).
# Put this file next to orders_story.csv.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv", dtype={"OrderID": str, "CustomerID": str, "Hub": str})
print(f"Rows imported = {len(df):,}")    # should be 10,000; never edit the CSV

def q_exc(x, p):
    """Excel QUARTILE.EXC / PERCENTILE.EXC: the (n + 1) * p position rule."""
    return np.percentile(x, 100 * p, method="weibull")

# ---- Part A: sentinel audit ----
print(f"Age sentinels (-1)      = {(df['Age_Years'] == -1).sum()}")
print(f"Latency sentinels (999) = {(df['Latency_Minutes'] == 999).sum()}")
# Read the OrderTier codes and decide the scale yourself.
print(df["OrderTier"].value_counts().sort_index())

# ---- Part B: center and spread of VALID latency ----
valid = df[(df["Latency_Minutes"] != 999) & df["Latency_Minutes"].notna()]
lat = valid["Latency_Minutes"]
q1, q3 = q_exc(lat, 0.25), q_exc(lat, 0.75)
print(f"Valid latency records   = {len(lat):,}")
print(f"Mean latency            = {lat.mean():.1f} min")
print(f"Median latency          = {lat.median():.1f} min")
print(f"Sample SD               = {lat.std(ddof=1):.1f} min")   # ddof=1 matches STDEV.S
print(f"IQR (Q3 - Q1)           = {q3 - q1:.1f} min")

# ---- Part C: Tukey fences ----
iqr = q3 - q1
upper, lower = q3 + 1.5 * iqr, q1 - 1.5 * iqr
print(f"Upper fence             = {upper:.1f} min")
print(f"Lower fence             = {lower:.1f} min")
print(f"Records above upper     = {(lat > upper).sum():,}")
top_two = lat.nlargest(2).to_numpy()
print(f"Largest valid latency   = {top_two[0]:.1f} min")
print(f"Second largest          = {top_two[1]:.1f} min")

# ---- Part D: grouped summary by hub (same valid-latency rule for every row) ----
def summary(x):
    a, b = q_exc(x, 0.25), q_exc(x, 0.75)
    return pd.Series({"Count": len(x), "Median": x.median(),
                      "Q1": a, "Q3": b, "IQR": b - a})

table = valid.groupby("Hub")["Latency_Minutes"].apply(summary).unstack()
table.loc["All Hubs"] = summary(lat)
print(table.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"))
hub_total = int(table.loc[["Hub A", "Hub B", "Hub C"], "Count"].sum())
print("Hub counts add up:", hub_total == len(lat))
R Parts A, B, C, D

The same checks in base R. quantile(type = 6) matches QUARTILE.EXC and SPSS HAVERAGE, and sd() matches STDEV.S.

# LAB01 Parts A-D in R (optional, not graded). Base R only.
# Put this file next to orders_story.csv.
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv",
               colClasses = c(OrderID = "character", CustomerID = "character", Hub = "character"))
cat("Rows imported =", nrow(df), "\n")    # should be 10000; never edit the CSV
# type 6 matches Excel QUARTILE.EXC and SPSS HAVERAGE
q_exc <- function(x, p) unname(quantile(x, p, type = 6))
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)

# ---- Part A: sentinel audit ----
cat("Age sentinels (-1)      =", sum(df$Age_Years == -1), "\n")
cat("Latency sentinels (999) =", sum(df$Latency_Minutes == 999), "\n")
# Read the OrderTier codes and decide the scale yourself.
print(table(OrderTier = df$OrderTier))

# ---- Part B: center and spread of VALID latency ----
valid <- df[!is.na(df$Latency_Minutes) & df$Latency_Minutes != 999, ]
lat <- valid$Latency_Minutes
q1 <- q_exc(lat, 0.25); q3 <- q_exc(lat, 0.75)
cat("Valid latency records   =", length(lat), "\n")
cat("Mean latency            =", f1(mean(lat)), "min\n")
cat("Median latency          =", f1(median(lat)), "min\n")
cat("Sample SD               =", f1(sd(lat)), "min\n")     # sd() divides by n - 1, like STDEV.S
cat("IQR (Q3 - Q1)           =", f1(q3 - q1), "min\n")

# ---- Part C: Tukey fences ----
iqr <- q3 - q1
upper <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr; lower <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
top_two <- sort(lat, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]
cat("Upper fence             =", f1(upper), "min\n")
cat("Lower fence             =", f1(lower), "min\n")
cat("Records above upper     =", sum(lat > upper), "\n")
cat("Largest valid latency   =", f1(top_two[1]), "min\n")
cat("Second largest          =", f1(top_two[2]), "min\n")

# ---- Part D: grouped summary by hub (same valid-latency rule for every row) ----
summ <- function(x) c(Count = length(x), Median = median(x),
                      Q1 = q_exc(x, 0.25), Q3 = q_exc(x, 0.75))
tab <- t(sapply(split(lat, valid$Hub), summ))
tab <- rbind(tab, "All Hubs" = summ(lat))
tab <- cbind(tab, IQR = tab[, "Q3"] - tab[, "Q1"])
print(round(tab, 1))
cat("Hub counts add up:", sum(tab[c("Hub A", "Hub B", "Hub C"), "Count"]) == length(lat), "\n")

EXAMINE VARIABLES=Latency_Minutes

Python Parts B

Pretend some 999 codes slipped past your screen. Add 10, 42, 100 and more of them, then watch the mean and the standard deviation climb while the median stays at 22.0 minutes. The chart is saved as resistance.png.

# Extension: resistance in action (Part B).
# Add extreme delays and watch the mean and the median.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv", dtype={"OrderID": str, "CustomerID": str, "Hub": str})
keep = (df["Latency_Minutes"] != 999) & df["Latency_Minutes"].notna()
lat = df.loc[keep, "Latency_Minutes"].to_numpy()

rows = []
for extra in [0, 10, 42, 100, 500, 1000]:
    x = np.append(lat, np.full(extra, 999.0))   # pretend 'extra' codes slipped in
    rows.append({"added 999s": extra, "mean": x.mean(),
                 "median": np.median(x), "sample SD": x.std(ddof=1)})
result = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(result.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"))

plt.plot(result["added 999s"], result["mean"], marker="o", label="Mean")
plt.plot(result["added 999s"], result["median"], marker="o", label="Median")
plt.xlabel("Number of 999 codes left in the data")
plt.ylabel("Minutes")
plt.title("The median resists bad codes; the mean does not")
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("resistance.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
print("Saved resistance.png. The 42 real sentinels are the row with 42 added.")
R Parts B

The same sweep in base R, with the chart saved as resistance_r.png. The row with 0 added should show the Part B mean and median.

# Extension: resistance in action. Add extreme delays and watch the mean and median (Part B)
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv",
               colClasses = c(OrderID = "character", CustomerID = "character", Hub = "character"))
lat <- df$Latency_Minutes[!is.na(df$Latency_Minutes) & df$Latency_Minutes != 999]
res <- data.frame()
for (extra in c(0, 10, 42, 100, 500, 1000)) {
  x <- c(lat, rep(999, extra))              # pretend 'extra' sentinel codes slipped in
  res <- rbind(res, data.frame(added = extra, mean = mean(x), median = median(x), sd = sd(x)))
}
print(round(res, 1))
png("resistance_r.png", width = 700, height = 450)
plot(res$added, res$mean, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = c(0, max(res$mean)),
     xlab = "Number of 999 codes left in the data", ylab = "Minutes",
     main = "The median resists bad codes; the mean does not")
lines(res$added, res$median, type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Mean", "Median"), pch = c(19, 1), lty = c(1, 2))
dev.off()
cat("Saved resistance_r.png. The 42 real sentinels are the row with 42 added.\n")

Topic 3 · How sensitive are the Tukey fences? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts C

In a copy of your workbook, add a new sheet. Step 1. Type 1.5, 2 and 3 in A2:A4. These are the multipliers k. Step 2. In B2 type ='IN-CLASS_Lab Part D'!$E$10+A2*'IN-CLASS_Lab Part D'!$F$10 and fill down to B4. Part D E10 is the all-hubs Q3 and F10 is the all-hubs IQR. Step 3. In C2 type =COUNTIFS(Orders[Latency_Minutes],"<>999",Orders[Latency_Minutes],">"&B2) and fill down. The <>999 criterion keeps the sentinel codes out. Step 4. Row 2 should match Part C: 49.0 minutes in B2 and 829 records in C2. How fast does the count fall as k grows?

SPSS Parts C

Builds one flag per multiplier from the H2 quartiles, then counts each flag. The 999 codes are user-missing, so they get no flag. Which multiplier would you defend to the VP, and why?

New code: paste it at the end of LAB01_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Extension: how many orders are flagged if the Tukey multiplier changes .
* Why: a flag count depends on the rule; see how fast it falls as the fence widens .
* How: 31 is the H2 HAVERAGE Q3 and 12 is the IQR (31 minus 19) .
* How: 999 is user-missing, so those rows get no flag in any column .
* Read the result: the value 1 row of Flag_k15 should match Part C B9 .
* Run: Run H0 first, then select this block and choose Run > Selection .
DATASET ACTIVATE OrdersData.
TITLE 'Extension Fence Sensitivity'.
COMPUTE Flag_k15=(Latency_Minutes > 31 + 1.5*12).
COMPUTE Flag_k2=(Latency_Minutes > 31 + 2*12).
COMPUTE Flag_k3=(Latency_Minutes > 31 + 3*12).
VARIABLE LABELS Flag_k15 'Above Q3 + 1.5 IQR'
 Flag_k2 'Above Q3 + 2 IQR'
 Flag_k3 'Above Q3 + 3 IQR'.
EXECUTE.
FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=Flag_k15 Flag_k2 Flag_k3.
Python Parts C

Prints the fence and the flag count for k = 1.5, 2 and 3, then charts the count for k from 1 to 3 as fence_sensitivity.png. The count axis starts at zero.

# Extension: how many orders are flagged if the Tukey multiplier changes? (Part C)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv", dtype={"OrderID": str, "CustomerID": str, "Hub": str})
valid = df[(df["Latency_Minutes"] != 999) & df["Latency_Minutes"].notna()]
lat = valid["Latency_Minutes"]
q1, q3 = np.percentile(lat, [25, 75], method="weibull")      # QUARTILE.EXC
iqr = q3 - q1

rows = []
for k in [1.5, 2, 3]:
    fence = q3 + k * iqr
    rows.append({"k": k, "upper fence": fence, "flagged": int((lat > fence).sum())})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"))

# A finer sweep for the chart: how fast does the flag count fall as k grows?
ks = np.arange(1.0, 3.01, 0.25)
counts = [int((lat > q3 + k * iqr).sum()) for k in ks]
plt.plot(ks, counts, marker="o", color="black")
plt.axvline(1.5, linestyle="--", color="gray", label="Tukey's 1.5")
plt.xlabel("Multiplier k in Q3 + k * IQR")
plt.ylabel("Valid orders flagged")
plt.ylim(bottom=0)
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("fence_sensitivity.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
print("Saved fence_sensitivity.png. At k = 1.5 you should see the Part C count.")
R Parts C

Recomputes the upper fence with multipliers 1.5, 2 and 3, and counts the flagged orders by hub each time. Which flags survive a stricter rule?

# Extension: how many orders are flagged if the Tukey multiplier changes? (Part C)
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv",
               colClasses = c(OrderID = "character", CustomerID = "character", Hub = "character"))
valid <- df[!is.na(df$Latency_Minutes) & df$Latency_Minutes != 999, ]
q <- unname(quantile(valid$Latency_Minutes, c(0.25, 0.75), type = 6))   # QUARTILE.EXC
iqr <- q[2] - q[1]
for (k in c(1.5, 2, 3)) {
  fence <- q[2] + k * iqr
  flagged <- valid$Latency_Minutes > fence
  cat(sprintf("\nk = %.1f: upper fence = %.1f min, flagged = %d of %d valid orders\n",
              k, fence, sum(flagged), nrow(valid)))
  print(table(Hub = factor(valid$Hub[flagged], levels = sort(unique(valid$Hub)))))
}
# A wider fence flags fewer orders. Which hubs still have flags at k = 3?

Python Parts C, D

Draws one histogram per hub with the same 10-minute bins and axes, prints the bin counts, and adds side-by-side boxplots. The bars touch because minutes are continuous. Do the hubs differ in the middle, in the tail, or both?

# Extension: histograms and boxplots by hub on one shared scale (Parts C and D).
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv", dtype={"OrderID": str, "CustomerID": str, "Hub": str})
valid = df[(df["Latency_Minutes"] != 999) & df["Latency_Minutes"].notna()]
bins = np.arange(0, 131, 10)                                 # same 10-minute bins for every hub

# Count table first: one row per 10-minute bin, one column per hub.
binned = pd.cut(valid["Latency_Minutes"], bins=bins, right=False)
print(pd.crosstab(valid["Hub"], binned, dropna=False).T.to_string())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, (hub, group) in zip(axes, valid.groupby("Hub")):
    # No gaps: the bins touch because minutes are continuous.
    ax.hist(group["Latency_Minutes"], bins=bins, color="gray", edgecolor="white")
    ax.axvline(group["Latency_Minutes"].median(), color="black", linestyle="--", label="median")
    ax.set_title(f"{hub} (n = {len(group):,} valid orders)", loc="left")
    ax.legend()
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Fulfillment latency (minutes)")
fig.suptitle("Same center, different tails?")
fig.savefig("hub_histograms.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")

# Boxplots on the same minute scale; the box edges use numpy's default quartiles.
hubs = sorted(valid["Hub"].unique())
fig2, ax2 = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax2.boxplot([valid.loc[valid["Hub"] == h, "Latency_Minutes"] for h in hubs], whis=1.5)
ax2.set_xticks(range(1, len(hubs) + 1))
ax2.set_xticklabels(hubs)
ax2.set_ylabel("Fulfillment latency (minutes)")
fig2.savefig("hub_boxplots.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
print("Saved hub_histograms.png and hub_boxplots.png.")
print("Compare the right tails, not only the medians.")
R Parts C, D

The same histograms in base R, plus a boxplot for each hub with the all-hubs upper fence as a dashed line. It prints the five numbers behind each box. R's box edges use Tukey hinges, so they can differ slightly from your QUARTILE.EXC values.

# Extension: histograms and boxplots of valid latency by hub (Parts C and D)
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv",
               colClasses = c(OrderID = "character", CustomerID = "character", Hub = "character"))
valid <- df[!is.na(df$Latency_Minutes) & df$Latency_Minutes != 999, ]
hubs <- sort(unique(valid$Hub))
brks <- seq(0, 130, by = 10)                   # same 10-minute bins for every hub
counts <- sapply(hubs, function(h)
  table(cut(valid$Latency_Minutes[valid$Hub == h], brks, right = FALSE)))
print(counts)                                  # one row per bin, one column per hub

png("hub_histograms_r.png", width = 700, height = 700)
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (h in hubs) {
  x <- valid$Latency_Minutes[valid$Hub == h]
  hist(x, breaks = brks, right = FALSE, ylim = c(0, max(counts)),
       col = "gray", border = "white", xlab = "Fulfillment latency (minutes)",
       main = paste0(h, " (n = ", length(x), " valid orders)"))
  abline(v = median(x), lty = 2)
}
par(op)
dev.off()

q <- unname(quantile(valid$Latency_Minutes, c(0.25, 0.75), type = 6))
upper <- q[2] + 1.5 * (q[2] - q[1])            # the all-hubs upper fence from Part C
png("hub_boxplots_r.png", width = 700, height = 400)
b <- boxplot(Latency_Minutes ~ Hub, data = valid, horizontal = TRUE,
             col = "gray90", xlab = "Fulfillment latency (minutes)", ylab = "",
             main = "Valid latency by hub")
abline(v = upper, lty = 2)
dev.off()
colnames(b$stats) <- b$names
rownames(b$stats) <- c("lower whisker", "lower hinge", "median",
                       "upper hinge", "upper whisker")
print(b$stats)
# R draws the box from Tukey hinges, so box edges can differ slightly from QUARTILE.EXC.
# Compare: exclusive Q1, median and Q3 for each hub, as in Part D.
exc <- sapply(split(valid$Latency_Minutes, valid$Hub),
              function(x) quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), type = 6))
print(exc)

Topic 5 · Where do the fence flags sit? Extend

Same question in Excel → SPSS → Python → R.

Excel Parts C, D

In a copy of your workbook, add a new sheet. Step 1. Type Hub A, Hub B and Hub C in A2:A4. Step 2. In B2 type =COUNTIFS(Orders[Hub],A2,Orders[Latency_Minutes],"<>999",Orders[Latency_Minutes],">"&'IN-CLASS_Lab Part C'!$B$7) and fill down to B4. Step 3. In C2 type =B2/'IN-CLASS_Lab Part D'!B7, fill down to C4, and format column C as Percentage. Part D rows 7 to 9 hold the valid counts for Hub A to Hub C, so the fill lines up. Step 4. Check that B2 + B3 + B4 equals Part C B9, the 829 flagged records. Then chart column C as a bar chart with the axis starting at 0%.

SPSS Parts C, D

Flags every valid order above the Part C upper fence, then crosstabs the flag by hub with row percentages. Is the tail spread across hubs or concentrated in one?

New code: paste it at the end of LAB01_SPSS.sps, make sure the setup has run this session, then select only the pasted lines and choose Run › Selection.

* Extension: which hubs hold the orders above the upper Tukey fence .
* Why: a count of flags is more useful when you know where the flags sit .
* How: 49 is the Part C B7 upper fence; 999 is user-missing, so those rows get no flag .
* Run: Run H0 first, then select this block and choose Run > Selection .
DATASET ACTIVATE OrdersData.
TITLE 'Extension Fence Flags by Hub'.
COMPUTE AboveFence=(Latency_Minutes > 49).
VALUE LABELS AboveFence 0 'At or below fence' 1 'Above fence'.
EXECUTE.
CROSSTABS
 /TABLES=Hub BY AboveFence
 /CELLS=COUNT ROW.
Python Parts C, D

Counts the flagged orders in each hub, then divides by that hub's own valid orders. The bar chart fence_flags_by_hub.png starts its axis at zero. The All Hubs row should match Part C B9.

# Extension: which hubs hold the orders above the upper Tukey fence? (Parts C and D)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("orders_story.csv", dtype={"OrderID": str, "CustomerID": str, "Hub": str})
valid = df[(df["Latency_Minutes"] != 999) & df["Latency_Minutes"].notna()].copy()
q1, q3 = np.percentile(valid["Latency_Minutes"], [25, 75], method="weibull")
upper = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)                                 # the Part C B7 fence, all hubs
valid["AboveFence"] = valid["Latency_Minutes"] > upper

counts = pd.crosstab(valid["Hub"], valid["AboveFence"], margins=True, margins_name="All Hubs")
shares = pd.crosstab(valid["Hub"], valid["AboveFence"], normalize="index") * 100
print(f"Upper fence = {upper:.1f} min")
print(counts.to_string())
print(shares.round(1).to_string())      # row percent within each hub

ax = shares[True].plot.bar(color="gray", rot=0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)                                          # an amount axis starts at zero
ax.set_ylabel("Percent of the hub's valid orders")
ax.set_title("Share of each hub above the all-hubs fence", loc="left")
plt.savefig("fence_flags_by_hub.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
print("Saved fence_flags_by_hub.png.")
R Parts C, D

The same count and row-percent tables in base R, with the bar chart saved as fence_flags_by_hub_r.png. The Sum row should match Part C B9.

# Extension: which hubs hold the orders above the upper Tukey fence? (Parts C and D)
df <- read.csv("orders_story.csv",
               colClasses = c(OrderID = "character", CustomerID = "character", Hub = "character"))
valid <- df[!is.na(df$Latency_Minutes) & df$Latency_Minutes != 999, ]
q <- unname(quantile(valid$Latency_Minutes, c(0.25, 0.75), type = 6))   # QUARTILE.EXC
upper <- q[2] + 1.5 * (q[2] - q[1])            # the Part C B7 fence, all hubs
above <- factor(valid$Latency_Minutes > upper, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                labels = c("At or below", "Above fence"))
tab <- table(Hub = valid$Hub, Fence = above)
cat("Upper fence =", sprintf("%.1f", upper), "min\n")
print(addmargins(tab, 1))                      # the Sum row should match Part C B9
share <- round(100 * prop.table(tab, 1), 1)    # row percent within each hub
print(share)
png("fence_flags_by_hub_r.png", width = 600, height = 400)
barplot(share[, "Above fence"], ylim = c(0, 100), col = "gray",
        ylab = "Percent of the hub's valid orders",
        main = "Share of each hub above the all-hubs fence")
dev.off()
